title: PoC weekly sync - latency stability / burst traffic traces
summary: Weekly PoC check-in focused on bursty traffic causing p95/p99 spikes and occasional timeouts. Customer walked through burst traffic traces (mixed context lengths, prefill+decode interleaving) and the observed GPU memory behavior. Redwood explained current understanding: KV cache fragmentation and allocator churn under bursts. Redwood outlined compaction project plan, feature-flagged canary rollout, and what metrics should improve (fragmentation ratio, allocation failures, eviction churn, and tail latency). Agreed on what data HelioPath will share (anonymized request mix + arrival patterns) and Redwood will share (dashboard panels, recommended alert thresholds, and a canary enablement checklist for the PoC pool).
topics: Customer burst traces: arrival patterns, queueing, long-context mix
Symptoms: p99 spikes, occasional OOM / admission control tightening
KV cache fragmentation: what it is, how it shows up, and why bursts make it worse
Compaction approach: feature flag, triggers, budgeting to avoid median latency regressions
Canary plan: region/pool scope, rollback signals, and reporting cadence
Metrics to watch: fragmentation ratio, allocation failures, compaction time/cost, eviction rate, p95/p99 per pool/model
questions: Can we guarantee compaction won’t increase average latency for steady-state workloads?
How will compaction interact with prefix caching / reuse?
What are the rollback levers if we see regressions in one model family?
Can we get per-tenant attribution for fragmentation pressure in a multi-tenant pool?

Redwood (Noah): Provide a short write-up of fragmentation ratio definition + how to interpret allocation failures by 2025-03-05
Redwood (Lauren): Schedule 30-min follow-up after traces are reviewed (target 2025-03-06 or 2025-03-07)
next_steps: Customer to upload burst trace artifacts (sanitized) and confirm PoC pool settings
Redwood to review traces against internal burst/mixed-length benchmark scenarios and report expected impact
Redwood to share canary enablement checklist + rollback criteria for compaction flag
Next sync to decide whether to enable compaction canary in HelioPath PoC pool (limited scope, daytime window)
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-03-01
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Title: PoC weekly sync - latency stability / burst traffic traces
Attendees: Lauren Bishop (Redwood), Noah Patel (Redwood), Rafael Mendes (Redwood), Priya Nair (HelioPath), Evan Cole (HelioPath), Jordan Lee (HelioPath)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- HelioPath shared burst traffic traces and showed p99 spikes correlated with high concurrency and mixed context lengths.
- Redwood explained likely KV cache fragmentation / allocator churn mechanism and outlined upcoming compaction canary plan.
- Agreed on concrete artifacts to exchange and a follow-up meeting after Redwood reviews traces.

00:00 Lauren Bishop: Hey everyone. Good to see you. Same agenda as usual, but I know you all said you had traces from the burst event earlier this week. Want to start there?

00:14 Priya Nair: Yep. I can share screen. So, we had a marketing email go out and the chatbot traffic jumped, like, 6x in about two minutes.

00:25 Jordan Lee: And it wasn’t just volume, it was like the mix changed. More long context because people were pasting big chunks.

00:31 Lauren Bishop: Okay.

00:33 Priya Nair: So, here’s the trace view. You can see request arrivals, then latency. The median is fine. The p95 goes from like 420ms to 1.6 seconds, and p99 hits 6 to 9 seconds for a few minutes.

00:49 Evan Cole: And a couple timeouts on our side because we cut at 10 seconds.

00:55 Noah Patel: That shape—median steady but tail exploding—yeah, that’s consistent with what we’ve been calling the fragmentation + reallocation churn pattern.

01:05 Jordan Lee: Can you say that again? Fragmentation, but like GPU fragmentation?

01:10 Noah Patel: Yeah. Specifically KV cache fragmentation inside the serving runtime. Not “CUDA heap fragmentation” exactly, but the cache blocks we use for attention state—holes appear as sequences finish or get evicted, and when you get a burst, the allocator starts doing more searching and sometimes has to reshuffle or allocate new segments. That’s where you get the long tail.

01:31 Priya Nair: So in our trace, you can see GPU memory used goes up but doesn’t come down quickly. It kind of sawtooths.

01:38 Rafael Mendes: Quick question, Priya—this is the PoC pool in your dedicated cluster, right? Not the hosted endpoint.

01:44 Priya Nair: Correct, this is the dedicated PoC pool you set us up with.

01:47 Rafael Mendes: Great.

01:49 Priya Nair: Here’s a specific window. At 12:07, there’s a spike. We also saw two “out of memory” events in logs, but the pod didn’t crash. It looked like the runtime rejected work.

02:02 Jordan Lee: Yeah it returned 503 with a “capacity” message. Not sure if that was admission control.

02:07 Noah Patel: That’s admission control protecting the GPU from hard OOM. It can happen if the cache manager predicts it can’t safely fit the next batch.

02:16 Lauren Bishop: That’s the thing we want to avoid for your use case—spiky consumer traffic.

02:21 Evan Cole: The weird part is we’re not maxing GPU compute. The SM utilization is like 55%.

02:27 Noah Patel: Exactly. This is memory-layout and allocator overhead rather than raw compute. Compute headroom doesn’t help if you can’t place the KV blocks efficiently.

02:37 Priya Nair: So what do you need from us? We can share this trace. We can’t share the raw prompts, but we can share lengths and timings.

02:45 Lauren Bishop: That’s perfect. If you can share arrival rates over time, context length histogram, plus concurrency, that helps us map to our internal scenarios.

02:55 Rafael Mendes: And the pool identifier + current knobs you’ve set—like max inflight, any custom admission control limits—so we can correlate.

03:03 Jordan Lee: We can do that.

03:05 Noah Patel: Can I ask, what’s your mix of context lengths? Like 4k, 8k, 32k?

03:10 Evan Cole: Normal is like 2k to 6k. During the burst, we saw a lot of 12k to 18k, and a handful of 28k. We cap at 32k.

03:20 Noah Patel: Okay. Mixed-length is a known trigger. When you interleave prefill and decode and you’ve got variable lengths, the allocator tends to leave holes.

03:30 Priya Nair: We noticed that “holes” word in the postmortem you shared last week. So compaction means… moving stuff around?

03:37 Noah Patel: Yeah, that’s the gist. Today, we allocate KV cache in blocks that are effectively pinned once placed for a sequence. When the sequence finishes, those blocks become free, but they’re scattered. Compaction adds the ability to move blocks (safely) so free space becomes contiguous again.

03:55 Jordan Lee: Moving KV blocks on GPU sounds scary.

03:58 Noah Patel: It is scary if you do it wrong. That’s why it’s behind a flag and has strict budgeting. We also only move when we can guarantee we’re not racing in-flight kernels.

04:09 Rafael Mendes: From SRE perspective, we treat it like a canary-only change until we see stable metrics for at least 24 hours.

04:16 Lauren Bishop: And to be clear, it doesn’t change model outputs. It’s entirely runtime memory management.

04:22 Evan Cole: What’s the status? Like, is this shipping next week or…

04:26 Lauren Bishop: So the project is in progress now. The current plan is: first, instrumentation everywhere. That’s basically done in our mainline. Then allocator refactor and compaction engine. Then we canary one region/pool first.

04:41 Priya Nair: For our PoC, what’s the earliest we could try it?

04:45 Noah Patel: I don’t want to overpromise, but if your PoC pool is okay being a canary target, we could potentially enable it in a controlled window once the flag is in the release train. Realistically, think “couple weeks,” not days.

04:59 Jordan Lee: What would we see improve? Just p99?

05:02 Noah Patel: Primary target is tail latency—p95/p99—and fewer allocation failures. Also fewer cases where admission control clamps down. You should see fragmentation ratio flatten out.

05:15 Priya Nair: Fragmentation ratio is a metric you have already?

05:18 Rafael Mendes: Not exposed in your dashboards today. We have internal counters. We’re adding a consistent metric: basically (free blocks that are unusable due to layout) over total free blocks. There’s some nuance.

05:32 Noah Patel: And we’ll expose the supporting metrics too: “allocation failures,” “evictions per second,” and “compaction cost”—like bytes moved and time spent.

05:45 Evan Cole: Compaction cost includes GPU copy time?

05:48 Noah Patel: Yes. It’s usually small compared to decode, but if you run it too aggressively, it can steal cycles and hurt median. That’s why we do budgets.

06:00 Lauren Bishop: And we’ll be transparent about the budget knobs. You can tune conservatively.

06:05 Jordan Lee: Okay. Can we talk about the canary plan? Like what triggers rollback.

06:10 Rafael Mendes: Yup. For canary we set explicit rollback signals. A few examples:
- p99 latency regression above threshold for more than N minutes
- allocation failure rate increasing
- compaction time exceeding budget (meaning it’s thrashing)
- GPU memory errors or elevated 5xx

06:29 Priya Nair: Do you page on that automatically?

06:31 Rafael Mendes: Internally yes. For your PoC we’ll coordinate with you. We can also set your alerting on your side if you want.

06:41 Evan Cole: When you say “thrashing” you mean it compacts then immediately fragments again?

06:46 Noah Patel: Exactly. If triggers are too sensitive, you compact constantly and it’s counterproductive.

06:53 Priya Nair: In our traces, the spikes were during the burst and then things recovered after about 8 minutes.

07:00 Noah Patel: That’s classic. Once the mix returns to normal and in-flight sequences drain, fragmentation pressure drops.

07:08 Lauren Bishop: The goal is that recovery happens faster and the peak tail is much lower.

07:13 Jordan Lee: Do you have any early numbers?

07:16 Noah Patel: From internal synthetic scenarios, yes, but I’d rather not quote them as a guarantee. We’ve seen p99 improvements on the “bursty-mix” benchmark when compaction is on with conservative budgets.

07:31 Priya Nair: Okay.

07:33 Evan Cole: Question on prefix caching. We’re using some prompt prefix reuse, right? Could compaction evict those more?

07:41 Noah Patel: Great question. Prefix cache interacts with this. In some cases, a “sticky” prefix cache can worsen fragmentation because it pins blocks. We’re adding policy hooks so the scheduler can signal pressure and we can choose eviction victims more intelligently.

07:58 Jordan Lee: Scheduler signals pressure meaning it tells the cache manager “we’re overloaded”?

08:03 Noah Patel: Yeah, roughly. It’s a contract: scheduler can indicate cache pressure, and the cache layer can push back with “I can’t admit this without eviction/compaction.” The key is fairness so one tenant doesn’t starve others.

08:18 Priya Nair: For our PoC, we’re single tenant, so fairness isn’t a big deal, but I get why you need it.

08:24 Lauren Bishop: Exactly. But the same mechanisms apply.

08:28 Priya Nair: Let me show the histograms. This is context length distribution during burst. (pause) You can see it shifts right.

08:39 Noah Patel: Yup.

08:41 Evan Cole: Another data point: token throughput drops. We go from 58k tokens/sec down to 31k.

08:47 Noah Patel: That’s because batching efficiency drops and you’re spending time on allocator/eviction overhead.

08:54 Jordan Lee: Also, we saw log lines like “search depth exceeded” in the allocator. I don’t know if that helps.

09:00 Noah Patel: That’s very helpful. That’s basically allocator scanning too many free segments.

09:06 Rafael Mendes: If you can paste a snippet of those log lines—sanitized—that helps us confirm.

09:11 Priya Nair: We can do that.

09:13 Lauren Bishop: Awesome. So, aligning on what we’ll send and what you’ll send. From our side, we’ll send dashboard panels—at least screenshots for now—and a doc on how to interpret fragmentation signals.

09:25 Jordan Lee: Can we get actual metric names? We want to wire it into our Grafana.

09:29 Rafael Mendes: For PoC, we can give you the metric names we expose in the dedicated telemetry stream. Some might be internal-only until the pack is finalized, but we can share what we have.

09:40 Evan Cole: And what’s the expected steady-state overhead with compaction on?

09:45 Noah Patel: If it’s configured correctly, basically near-zero on median. Compaction should run only when fragmentation is high or on allocation failure. But there is always some overhead when it runs—GPU copies and synchronization.

10:00 Priya Nair: Synchronization meaning it pauses kernels?

10:03 Noah Patel: It can require stream sync points to ensure pointers are stable. We’re trying to minimize those. Some parts can be overlapped.

10:14 Jordan Lee: So worst case you introduce a stall.

10:17 Noah Patel: Worst case, yes. That’s why budgets.

10:20 Lauren Bishop: And that’s why canary with rollback.

10:23 Priya Nair: What does “budget” look like? Time per minute?

10:27 Noah Patel: Could be time-based and/or bytes moved per interval. Like “no more than X ms of compaction work per second.” We’re still tuning. We also have a fallback mode: only compact when allocation fails.

10:44 Evan Cole: That might be safer for us.

10:46 Noah Patel: It tends to reduce tail, but not as much as proactive compaction. Tradeoffs.

10:53 Priya Nair: In the burst case, allocation failures already happen though.

10:56 Noah Patel: Right. If you wait for failure, you may still see a spike, but the recovery is better. Proactive keeps you from hitting the cliff.

11:08 Rafael Mendes: From operations, we usually start with conservative triggers and raise them gradually.

11:14 Jordan Lee: Okay.

11:16 Priya Nair: Another question: is this specific to one model? We were using Llama 3 variant.

11:22 Noah Patel: Fragmentation can be worse depending on head count, layer count, and how we lay out KV blocks. Some model families have different block footprints.

11:33 Evan Cole: We also tested a smaller model and didn’t see the same spikes.

11:36 Noah Patel: That makes sense.

11:39 Lauren Bishop: For the PoC success criteria you shared—stable p99 under bursts—this is the exact initiative we’re doing.

11:49 Priya Nair: Great, but we have an internal deadline end of month.

11:53 Lauren Bishop: Understood. What I can commit to is: we’ll review your traces this week, we’ll share the canary plan and metrics within a few days, and if the flag is ready in the PoC release train, we’ll target a controlled canary in your pool as soon as practical.

12:10 Jordan Lee: If it’s not ready, what’s the mitigation? Just more admission control?

12:14 Rafael Mendes: Today, mitigations are basically:
- reduce max concurrency
- cap max context or route long-context to a separate pool
- adjust batching settings
- tighten prefix cache limits
But those trade throughput for stability.

12:30 Priya Nair: We did route some long-context traffic away, but it complicates product.

12:35 Evan Cole: And we don’t want to degrade output.

12:37 Noah Patel: Totally. That’s why the longer-term fix is compaction.

12:43 Priya Nair: Can you explain how you’ll attribute tail latency to compaction events? Like, I want to know “this spike is because compaction ran.”

12:52 Noah Patel: We’re adding structured events: compaction start/stop with moved-bytes and a reason code (threshold trigger vs allocation failure). Then per-request, we can at least correlate if it overlapped.

13:07 Rafael Mendes: And we’ll chart compaction time and fragmentation ratio alongside p99. It becomes pretty obvious.

13:14 Jordan Lee: Okay.

13:16 Lauren Bishop: Priya, could you send the artifact in whatever format is easiest? CSV is fine.

13:21 Priya Nair: Yep. We have a sanitized export.

13:23 Evan Cole: For request IDs, we can generate fake IDs, but we can include timings.

13:27 Noah Patel: That’s fine. We mostly need distributions.

13:32 Priya Nair: One more note: our burst was not perfectly random; it came in waves every ~20 seconds.

13:39 Noah Patel: That’s interesting. That wave pattern can worsen fragmentation because you get synchronized sequence completions, then new allocations.

13:49 Jordan Lee: Like churn cycles.

13:51 Noah Patel: Exactly.

13:55 Lauren Bishop: Can I pivot briefly—any other PoC blockers besides latency stability?

14:00 Priya Nair: Mostly that. Security review is ongoing but fine. We’re okay on network.

14:05 Evan Cole: Also cost, but we’ll evaluate once latency is stable.

14:10 Lauren Bishop: Great. We’ll keep this scoped.

14:13 Rafael Mendes: Quick ops check: are you collecting GPU memory stats per second? Or just from DCGM at 15s?

14:19 Jordan Lee: We have DCGM at 10 seconds.

14:22 Rafael Mendes: If you can temporarily raise to 1s during the next test, it helps pinpoint the stall moments. Totally optional.

14:30 Jordan Lee: We can do 2s maybe. 1s is a lot.

14:33 Rafael Mendes: 2s works.

14:35 Noah Patel: Another request: can you note whether prefill and decode are on the same queue? Some setups separate them.

14:41 Priya Nair: I think same queue right now.

14:44 Evan Cole: Yes, same endpoint, same pool.

14:46 Noah Patel: That can contribute. Separating can improve predictability but might reduce utilization. Not suggesting you change it yet.

14:56 Priya Nair: Okay.

15:00 Lauren Bishop: Let’s talk about canary specifics so you know what to expect. The canary will be a runtime flag: compaction enabled, with a conservative budget. We’ll enable it in a limited slice of traffic/pods.

15:15 Jordan Lee: Like 10%?

15:16 Rafael Mendes: Usually start with one pod, then 10%, then 25%. For dedicated we can do it at pool-level by selecting nodes.

15:26 Priya Nair: And if it goes wrong we flip the flag off.

15:29 Rafael Mendes: Yup. Rollback is immediate. Also you can revert to previous runtime build if needed.

15:36 Evan Cole: How quickly does rollback take effect? In-flight requests?

15:40 Noah Patel: New requests stop using compaction immediately. In-flight sequences keep their current allocation. There’s no model restart required.

15:48 Jordan Lee: Good.

15:50 Priya Nair: What metrics will you show us during canary?

15:54 Rafael Mendes: The main ones:
- fragmentation ratio (per GPU / per pool)
- allocation failure count (per minute)
- eviction rate
- compaction time (ms/sec) and bytes moved
- p95/p99 latency broken out by model and endpoint

16:15 Priya Nair: Okay.

16:16 Evan Cole: Can you include throughput? tokens/sec.

16:19 Rafael Mendes: Yes.

16:21 Noah Patel: Also we’ll watch for median regressions—p50 and p90.

16:26 Priya Nair: Great.

16:28 Jordan Lee: Do you anticipate any weird issues with “pointer stability”? I saw that phrase in one of your emails.

16:35 Noah Patel: Yeah. The main correctness risk is moving a block while a kernel is reading it. We prevent that with stream synchronization and versioning metadata. We also have stress tests. But canary is the real proof.

16:49 Evan Cole: Okay.

16:51 Lauren Bishop: I’m going to capture next steps before we run out of time.

16:55 Priya Nair: Sure.

17:00 Lauren Bishop: From you all: send anonymized traces—arrival rate and context histograms—plus any relevant allocator logs and the pool config. Target Tuesday?

17:10 Priya Nair: Tuesday works.

17:12 Jordan Lee: I can send pool config Monday.

17:14 Lauren Bishop: Great.

17:16 Lauren Bishop: From us: Rafael will send dashboard screenshots and proposed alert thresholds; Noah will send a short write-up on fragmentation ratio and allocation failure interpretation.

17:26 Rafael Mendes: Yep.

17:27 Noah Patel: Yep.

17:29 Evan Cole: Can we also get a rough timeline on when the flag is available in dedicated?

17:34 Lauren Bishop: I’ll check with release coordination and send you an update in email. But plan on “mid-month” as a working estimate.

17:43 Priya Nair: Okay.

17:45 Jordan Lee: If we do a daytime canary, we want someone from Redwood on the hook.

17:49 Rafael Mendes: Agreed. We’ll schedule it with coverage.

17:52 Lauren Bishop: We’ll do that.

18:00 (crosstalk)
Priya Nair: One last thing—during the burst, we saw some requests stuck “queued” even though compute wasn’t full.
Noah Patel: That can happen if scheduler is backpressuring due to cache pressure. That’s actually a safety feature.
Jordan Lee: So compaction should reduce backpressure?
Noah Patel: It should reduce the frequency of hitting pressure thresholds.

18:22 Evan Cole: That’s good.

18:24 Lauren Bishop: Anything else before we wrap?

18:27 Priya Nair: No, this was good.

18:29 Jordan Lee: All set.

18:31 Evan Cole: Thanks.

18:32 Lauren Bishop: Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up with the materials and schedule the next sync.
